questions.scenario: One job contains checkout, installation, lint, and tests as ordered steps on the same worker. A reviewer asks to reinstall project dependencies before each command because they are different steps. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Install before every command because each step necessarily gets a new worker.
Prepare dependencies once in this job; another isolated job needs its own preparation.
Move dependencies into a report artifact and remove project declarations.
Depend on the developer laptop's installation to avoid worker setup.

questions.explanation: Steps in this job share its workspace. Repeating installation before every check is unnecessary. Separate isolated jobs need explicit preparation or appropriate data transfer; neither a report nor a laptop installation supplies that contract. [Official reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/get-started/understand-github-actions).

questions.scenario: The packaging job writes a release bundle. A later job depends on it, but that job's fresh workspace contains no bundle. Which repair addresses both the scheduling and data requirements?

options.text: Keep the dependency, publish the bundle, and retrieve it in the consumer.
Remove the dependency so both workers can search for the file at once.
Give both jobs the same display name to make their files shared.
Rebuild a different bundle downstream and treat it as the original output.

questions.explanation: A dependency orders work; artifact publication and retrieval move outputs. Names do not create shared storage, concurrent execution does not transfer files, and a new build does not prove consumption of the original package. [Official reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/writing-workflows/choosing-what-your-workflow-does/storing-and-sharing-data-from-a-workflow).

questions.scenario: A dependency cache is evicted overnight. The repository still contains its dependency declarations and reviewed lockfile. What should a correctly designed workflow do?

options.text: Deploy the previous cached package without validating the current checkout.
Treat cache absence as evidence that the source change is unsafe.
Reconstruct the locked dependencies, accepting a slower run.
Resolve a new dependency graph and overwrite the committed lock.

questions.explanation: A disposable dependency cache accelerates reconstruction; it should not determine logical correctness. Its loss neither invalidates source nor authorizes a new dependency graph or reuse of an unrelated release package. [Official reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching).

questions.scenario: A unit-test job fails, and its report-publication operation is skipped with the downstream success-only work. Engineers can see the red status but not the assertion failures. What should change?

options.text: Suppress the failure so the normal success path can publish reports.
Store only successful reports because failed results cannot inform debugging.
Make deployment run despite failure so its logs replace the missing report.
Publish diagnostic reports on failure while keeping release work blocked.

questions.explanation: Failure evidence is valuable precisely when tests fail. Publication can have its own completion behavior without converting failure into success or relaxing release gates. Deployment logs are not a replacement for the test report. [Official reference](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/pipeline/syntax/#post).

questions.scenario: The team has four outputs: downloaded dependency archives, a tested release binary, a coverage report needed for review, and regenerable intermediate compilation files. Which two need artifact-style retention for the stated purpose?

options.text: The tested release binary that downstream deployment must consume.
Downloaded archives used only to avoid fetching locked dependencies again.
The coverage report that reviewers must inspect after the run.
Intermediate files whose loss merely makes compilation slower.

questions.explanation: The release binary and review report are outputs/evidence to retain or transfer. The other two are regenerable acceleration data. A cache should not become the sole record of the release or its review evidence. [Official reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching).
